case_info.scenario: A 6-year-old boy with no relevant medical history presented to the pediatric dermatology clinic with a congenital scalp lesion. On physical exploration, an oval, indurated skin-colored plaque with overlying alopecia was observed on the occipital region (Figure 1A). A skin biopsy was performed for histopathological study (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, A firm, skin-toned oval plaque with localized hair loss was noted in the occipital area, consistent with the hair collar sign. B, Panoramic imaging of the biopsy is observed (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×4).
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed multiple dilated pseudovascular spaces in the mid and deep dermis, located between dermal collagen bundles. These were accompanied by an increased number of small, round cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, showing no atypia or mitotic activity (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that these cells were positive for epithelial membrane antigen and progesterone receptors, and negative for vascular markers such as CD31 and CD34. In view of the clinical stability of the lesion, the patient’s family opted against surgical intervention. Soft-tissue lesions of the scalp are common in clinical practice, with lipomas and trichilemmal cysts being among the most frequent. In children, common scalp lesions include dermoid cysts, infantile hemangiomas, and nevus sebaceous. Less common diagnoses are meningoceles, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, myofibromas, and hematologic neoplasms. Meningothelial hamartoma was first described in 1990 as a rare lesion, also known as a rudimentary meningocele.1Since then, 28 cases have been reported in the literature.2-8The presence of meningothelial cells outside of the central nervous system is an exceptional phenomenon. In meningothelial hamartomas, these cells are located in the skin, usually on the scalp, without extending beyond the subcutaneous tissue. The lesion contains multiple tissue types, including connective, vascular, and meningothelial components. In most patients, these lesions present as solitary, well-circumscribed nodules with overlying alopecia, exhibiting a skin-colored, reddish, or grayish hue. Although congenital, they are often detected in childhood or adulthood and may enlarge or cause pain. The hair collar sign should alert clinicians to the possible presence of ectopic neural tissue, with or without underlying central nervous system abnormalities.2,9 Since the clinical appearance of these lesions is nonspecific, diagnosis relies on histological analysis.1,9The differential diagnoses of meningothelial hamartomas include several mesenchymal neoplasms, such as angiosarcoma, spindle cell hemangioendothelioma, epithelioid hemangioma, giant cell fibroblastoma, and intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia. Meningothelial hamartomas arise in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue and are characterized histologically by connective tissue proliferation and small to medium caliber blood vessels intermixed with meningothelial elements. In histopathology, meningothelial elements refer to meningothelial cells, which are specialized cells that line the meninges, particularly the inner layer of the arachnoid and the arachnoid granulations. These cells appear oval to round with eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged in whorled patterns or surrounding pseudovascular spaces. Histological studies show no evidence of malignant transformation, such as nuclear atypia or increased mitotic activity. The epidermis overlying the lesion is usually histologically normal.5,10 Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically shows epidermal involvement with infiltration of Langerhans cells, which are S-100 and CD1a positive—findings not observed in this case. Aplasia cutis presents as an absence of skin at birth, usually ulcerated or scarlike, without dermal pseudovascular spaces or cellular proliferation. Spindle cell hemangioendothelioma is a vascular neoplasm characterized by spindle cells and vascular markers such as CD31, WT1, or GLUT1, all negative in this case. In contrast, the presence of uniform meningothelial-like cells arranged around pseudovascular spaces, along with positive staining for epithelial membrane antigen and progesterone receptors and absence of vascular, muscular, and neural markers, supports the diagnosis of meningothelial hamartoma. The negativity for S-100 aligns with the hypothesis that these lesions, despite a possible neural crest origin, do not express typical neural markers, helping to confirm the diagnosis of meningothelial hamartoma. While imaging such as magnetic resonance imaging can be useful to rule out deeper connections in suspected cases, in this patient, no neurological symptoms or bone abnormalities were observed clinically. Given the lesion’s confinement to the dermis and subcutis on histology, imaging was not deemed necessary, consistent with the approach reported in the literature. It is not necessary to perform additional complementary tests, as no associated pathologies have been described to date. Complete surgical excision of the meningothelial hamartoma is usually curative.1 Meningothelial hamartoma is an extremely rare, benign lesion that may be mistaken for a low-grade vascular neoplasm due to its unusual histological characteristics. Recognizing this lesion is crucial to avoid misclassification.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.scenario: A 6-year-old boy with no relevant medical history presented to the pediatric dermatology clinic with a congenital scalp lesion. On physical exploration, an oval, indurated skin-colored plaque with overlying alopecia was observed on the occipital region (Figure 1A). A skin biopsy was performed for histopathological study (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, A firm, skin-toned oval plaque with localized hair loss was noted in the occipital area, consistent with the hair collar sign. B, Panoramic imaging of the biopsy is observed (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×4).
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed multiple dilated pseudovascular spaces in the mid and deep dermis, located between dermal collagen bundles. These were accompanied by an increased number of small, round cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, showing no atypia or mitotic activity (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that these cells were positive for epithelial membrane antigen and progesterone receptors, and negative for vascular markers such as CD31 and CD34. In view of the clinical stability of the lesion, the patient’s family opted against surgical intervention. Soft-tissue lesions of the scalp are common in clinical practice, with lipomas and trichilemmal cysts being among the most frequent. In children, common scalp lesions include dermoid cysts, infantile hemangiomas, and nevus sebaceous. Less common diagnoses are meningoceles, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, myofibromas, and hematologic neoplasms. Meningothelial hamartoma was first described in 1990 as a rare lesion, also known as a rudimentary meningocele.1Since then, 28 cases have been reported in the literature.2-8The presence of meningothelial cells outside of the central nervous system is an exceptional phenomenon. In meningothelial hamartomas, these cells are located in the skin, usually on the scalp, without extending beyond the subcutaneous tissue. The lesion contains multiple tissue types, including connective, vascular, and meningothelial components. In most patients, these lesions present as solitary, well-circumscribed nodules with overlying alopecia, exhibiting a skin-colored, reddish, or grayish hue. Although congenital, they are often detected in childhood or adulthood and may enlarge or cause pain. The hair collar sign should alert clinicians to the possible presence of ectopic neural tissue, with or without underlying central nervous system abnormalities.2,9 Since the clinical appearance of these lesions is nonspecific, diagnosis relies on histological analysis.1,9The differential diagnoses of meningothelial hamartomas include several mesenchymal neoplasms, such as angiosarcoma, spindle cell hemangioendothelioma, epithelioid hemangioma, giant cell fibroblastoma, and intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia. Meningothelial hamartomas arise in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue and are characterized histologically by connective tissue proliferation and small to medium caliber blood vessels intermixed with meningothelial elements. In histopathology, meningothelial elements refer to meningothelial cells, which are specialized cells that line the meninges, particularly the inner layer of the arachnoid and the arachnoid granulations. These cells appear oval to round with eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged in whorled patterns or surrounding pseudovascular spaces. Histological studies show no evidence of malignant transformation, such as nuclear atypia or increased mitotic activity. The epidermis overlying the lesion is usually histologically normal.5,10 Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically shows epidermal involvement with infiltration of Langerhans cells, which are S-100 and CD1a positive—findings not observed in this case. Aplasia cutis presents as an absence of skin at birth, usually ulcerated or scarlike, without dermal pseudovascular spaces or cellular proliferation. Spindle cell hemangioendothelioma is a vascular neoplasm characterized by spindle cells and vascular markers such as CD31, WT1, or GLUT1, all negative in this case. In contrast, the presence of uniform meningothelial-like cells arranged around pseudovascular spaces, along with positive staining for epithelial membrane antigen and progesterone receptors and absence of vascular, muscular, and neural markers, supports the diagnosis of meningothelial hamartoma. The negativity for S-100 aligns with the hypothesis that these lesions, despite a possible neural crest origin, do not express typical neural markers, helping to confirm the diagnosis of meningothelial hamartoma. While imaging such as magnetic resonance imaging can be useful to rule out deeper connections in suspected cases, in this patient, no neurological symptoms or bone abnormalities were observed clinically. Given the lesion’s confinement to the dermis and subcutis on histology, imaging was not deemed necessary, consistent with the approach reported in the literature. It is not necessary to perform additional complementary tests, as no associated pathologies have been described to date. Complete surgical excision of the meningothelial hamartoma is usually curative.1 Meningothelial hamartoma is an extremely rare, benign lesion that may be mistaken for a low-grade vascular neoplasm due to its unusual histological characteristics. Recognizing this lesion is crucial to avoid misclassification.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact

- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

1. Mental Demand

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting

       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and

       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or

       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of

   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

Determine the relation between the clinician's claim and the medically established facts for the case.

{
  "overall_relation": "supported" | "contradicted" | "insufficient" | "mixed" | "unknown",

  "reasoning": "<substantive clinical reasoning, 3-5 sentences>",

}

facts that decide this case, WHY the clinician's claim holds this relation, and specifically what the
clinician is getting right, getting wrong, or missing. This reasoning is handed to the dialogue policy as
its grounded environment knowledge, so make it clinically informative, not merely a verdict.
For "confidence": how certain you are in this relation given the available evidence.

Relation definitions:
- supported: The clinician's claim is consistent with established medical evidence for this case.
- contradicted: The clinician's claim conflicts with established medical evidence.
- insufficient: There is not enough information to verify the claim.
- mixed: Parts of the claim are supported, parts are contradicted or unclear.

case_info.scenario: A 6-year-old boy with no relevant medical history presented to the pediatric dermatology clinic with a congenital scalp lesion. On physical exploration, an oval, indurated skin-colored plaque with overlying alopecia was observed on the occipital region (Figure 1A). A skin biopsy was performed for histopathological study (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, A firm, skin-toned oval plaque with localized hair loss was noted in the occipital area, consistent with the hair collar sign. B, Panoramic imaging of the biopsy is observed (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×4).
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed multiple dilated pseudovascular spaces in the mid and deep dermis, located between dermal collagen bundles. These were accompanied by an increased number of small, round cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, showing no atypia or mitotic activity (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that these cells were positive for epithelial membrane antigen and progesterone receptors, and negative for vascular markers such as CD31 and CD34. In view of the clinical stability of the lesion, the patient’s family opted against surgical intervention. Soft-tissue lesions of the scalp are common in clinical practice, with lipomas and trichilemmal cysts being among the most frequent. In children, common scalp lesions include dermoid cysts, infantile hemangiomas, and nevus sebaceous. Less common diagnoses are meningoceles, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, myofibromas, and hematologic neoplasms. Meningothelial hamartoma was first described in 1990 as a rare lesion, also known as a rudimentary meningocele.1Since then, 28 cases have been reported in the literature.2-8The presence of meningothelial cells outside of the central nervous system is an exceptional phenomenon. In meningothelial hamartomas, these cells are located in the skin, usually on the scalp, without extending beyond the subcutaneous tissue. The lesion contains multiple tissue types, including connective, vascular, and meningothelial components. In most patients, these lesions present as solitary, well-circumscribed nodules with overlying alopecia, exhibiting a skin-colored, reddish, or grayish hue. Although congenital, they are often detected in childhood or adulthood and may enlarge or cause pain. The hair collar sign should alert clinicians to the possible presence of ectopic neural tissue, with or without underlying central nervous system abnormalities.2,9 Since the clinical appearance of these lesions is nonspecific, diagnosis relies on histological analysis.1,9The differential diagnoses of meningothelial hamartomas include several mesenchymal neoplasms, such as angiosarcoma, spindle cell hemangioendothelioma, epithelioid hemangioma, giant cell fibroblastoma, and intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia. Meningothelial hamartomas arise in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue and are characterized histologically by connective tissue proliferation and small to medium caliber blood vessels intermixed with meningothelial elements. In histopathology, meningothelial elements refer to meningothelial cells, which are specialized cells that line the meninges, particularly the inner layer of the arachnoid and the arachnoid granulations. These cells appear oval to round with eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged in whorled patterns or surrounding pseudovascular spaces. Histological studies show no evidence of malignant transformation, such as nuclear atypia or increased mitotic activity. The epidermis overlying the lesion is usually histologically normal.5,10 Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically shows epidermal involvement with infiltration of Langerhans cells, which are S-100 and CD1a positive—findings not observed in this case. Aplasia cutis presents as an absence of skin at birth, usually ulcerated or scarlike, without dermal pseudovascular spaces or cellular proliferation. Spindle cell hemangioendothelioma is a vascular neoplasm characterized by spindle cells and vascular markers such as CD31, WT1, or GLUT1, all negative in this case. In contrast, the presence of uniform meningothelial-like cells arranged around pseudovascular spaces, along with positive staining for epithelial membrane antigen and progesterone receptors and absence of vascular, muscular, and neural markers, supports the diagnosis of meningothelial hamartoma. The negativity for S-100 aligns with the hypothesis that these lesions, despite a possible neural crest origin, do not express typical neural markers, helping to confirm the diagnosis of meningothelial hamartoma. While imaging such as magnetic resonance imaging can be useful to rule out deeper connections in suspected cases, in this patient, no neurological symptoms or bone abnormalities were observed clinically. Given the lesion’s confinement to the dermis and subcutis on histology, imaging was not deemed necessary, consistent with the approach reported in the literature. It is not necessary to perform additional complementary tests, as no associated pathologies have been described to date. Complete surgical excision of the meningothelial hamartoma is usually curative.1 Meningothelial hamartoma is an extremely rare, benign lesion that may be mistaken for a low-grade vascular neoplasm due to its unusual histological characteristics. Recognizing this lesion is crucial to avoid misclassification.

messages.content:
You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",

  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",

}

case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed multiple dilated pseudovascular spaces in the mid and deep dermis, located between dermal collagen bundles. These were accompanied by an increased number of small, round cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, showing no atypia or mitotic activity (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that these cells were positive for epithelial membrane antigen and progesterone receptors, and negative for vascular markers such as CD31 and CD34. Soft-tissue lesions of the scalp are common in clinical practice, with lipomas and trichilemmal cysts being among the most frequent. In children, common scalp lesions include dermoid cysts, infantile hemangiomas, and nevus sebaceous. Less common diagnoses are meningoceles, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, myofibromas, and hematologic neoplasms. Meningothelial hamartoma was first described in 1990 as a rare lesion, also known as a rudimentary meningocele.1Since then, 28 cases have been reported in the literature.2-8The presence of meningothelial cells outside of the central nervous system is an exceptional phenomenon. In meningothelial hamartomas, these cells are located in the skin, usually on the scalp, without extending beyond the subcutaneous tissue. The lesion contains multiple tissue types, including connective, vascular, and meningothelial components. In most patients, these lesions present as solitary, well-circumscribed nodules with overlying alopecia, exhibiting a skin-colored, reddish, or grayish hue. Although congenital, they are often detected in childhood or adulthood and may enlarge or cause pain. The hair collar sign should alert clinicians to the possible presence of ectopic neural tissue, with or without underlying central nervous system abnormalities.2,9 Since the clinical appearance of these lesions is nonspecific, diagnosis relies on histological analysis.1,9The differential diagnoses of meningothelial hamartomas include several mesenchymal neoplasms, such as angiosarcoma, spindle cell hemangioendothelioma, epithelioid hemangioma, giant cell fibroblastoma, and intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia. Meningothelial hamartomas arise in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue and are characterized histologically by connective tissue proliferation and small to medium caliber blood vessels intermixed with meningothelial elements. In histopathology, meningothelial elements refer to meningothelial cells, which are specialized cells that line the meninges, particularly the inner layer of the arachnoid and the arachnoid granulations. These cells appear oval to round with eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged in whorled patterns or surrounding pseudovascular spaces. Histological studies show no evidence of malignant transformation, such as nuclear atypia or increased mitotic activity. The epidermis overlying the lesion is usually histologically normal.5,10 Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically shows epidermal involvement with infiltration of Langerhans cells, which are S-100 and CD1a positive—findings not observed in this case. Aplasia cutis presents as an absence of skin at birth, usually ulcerated or scarlike, without dermal pseudovascular spaces or cellular proliferation. Spindle cell hemangioendothelioma is a vascular neoplasm characterized by spindle cells and vascular markers such as CD31, WT1, or GLUT1, all negative in this case. In contrast, the presence of uniform meningothelial-like cells arranged around pseudovascular spaces, along with positive staining for epithelial membrane antigen and progesterone receptors and absence of vascular, muscular, and neural markers, supports the diagnosis of meningothelial hamartoma. The negativity for S-100 aligns with the hypothesis that these lesions, despite a possible neural crest origin, do not express typical neural markers, helping to confirm the diagnosis of meningothelial hamartoma. While imaging such as magnetic resonance imaging can be useful to rule out deeper connections in suspected cases, in this patient, no neurological symptoms or bone abnormalities were observed clinically. Given the lesion’s confinement to the dermis and subcutis on histology, imaging was not deemed necessary, consistent with the approach reported in the literature. It is not necessary to perform additional complementary tests, as no associated pathologies have been described to date. Complete surgical excision of the meningothelial hamartoma is usually curative.1 Meningothelial hamartoma is an extremely rare, benign lesion that may be mistaken for a low-grade vascular neoplasm due to its unusual histological characteristics. Recognizing this lesion is crucial to avoid misclassification.

You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

case_info.scenario: A 6-year-old boy with no relevant medical history presented to the pediatric dermatology clinic with a congenital scalp lesion. On physical exploration, an oval, indurated skin-colored plaque with overlying alopecia was observed on the occipital region (Figure 1A). A skin biopsy was performed for histopathological study (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, A firm, skin-toned oval plaque with localized hair loss was noted in the occipital area, consistent with the hair collar sign. B, Panoramic imaging of the biopsy is observed (hematoxylin-eosin staining; original magnification ×4).
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed multiple dilated pseudovascular spaces in the mid and deep dermis, located between dermal collagen bundles. These were accompanied by an increased number of small, round cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, showing no atypia or mitotic activity (Figure 2). Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that these cells were positive for epithelial membrane antigen and progesterone receptors, and negative for vascular markers such as CD31 and CD34. In view of the clinical stability of the lesion, the patient’s family opted against surgical intervention. Soft-tissue lesions of the scalp are common in clinical practice, with lipomas and trichilemmal cysts being among the most frequent. In children, common scalp lesions include dermoid cysts, infantile hemangiomas, and nevus sebaceous. Less common diagnoses are meningoceles, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, myofibromas, and hematologic neoplasms. Meningothelial hamartoma was first described in 1990 as a rare lesion, also known as a rudimentary meningocele.1Since then, 28 cases have been reported in the literature.2-8The presence of meningothelial cells outside of the central nervous system is an exceptional phenomenon. In meningothelial hamartomas, these cells are located in the skin, usually on the scalp, without extending beyond the subcutaneous tissue. The lesion contains multiple tissue types, including connective, vascular, and meningothelial components. In most patients, these lesions present as solitary, well-circumscribed nodules with overlying alopecia, exhibiting a skin-colored, reddish, or grayish hue. Although congenital, they are often detected in childhood or adulthood and may enlarge or cause pain. The hair collar sign should alert clinicians to the possible presence of ectopic neural tissue, with or without underlying central nervous system abnormalities.2,9 Since the clinical appearance of these lesions is nonspecific, diagnosis relies on histological analysis.1,9The differential diagnoses of meningothelial hamartomas include several mesenchymal neoplasms, such as angiosarcoma, spindle cell hemangioendothelioma, epithelioid hemangioma, giant cell fibroblastoma, and intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia. Meningothelial hamartomas arise in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue and are characterized histologically by connective tissue proliferation and small to medium caliber blood vessels intermixed with meningothelial elements. In histopathology, meningothelial elements refer to meningothelial cells, which are specialized cells that line the meninges, particularly the inner layer of the arachnoid and the arachnoid granulations. These cells appear oval to round with eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged in whorled patterns or surrounding pseudovascular spaces. Histological studies show no evidence of malignant transformation, such as nuclear atypia or increased mitotic activity. The epidermis overlying the lesion is usually histologically normal.5,10 Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically shows epidermal involvement with infiltration of Langerhans cells, which are S-100 and CD1a positive—findings not observed in this case. Aplasia cutis presents as an absence of skin at birth, usually ulcerated or scarlike, without dermal pseudovascular spaces or cellular proliferation. Spindle cell hemangioendothelioma is a vascular neoplasm characterized by spindle cells and vascular markers such as CD31, WT1, or GLUT1, all negative in this case. You are a deliberation policy planner for a medical AI assisting a clinician toward the
best decision. You do NOT talk to the clinician yourself — each turn you choose the next
deliberation move (stage + locution) and write behavioral guidance for the medical AI.

Treat this as a PARTIALLY OBSERVABLE planning problem, not a reflex:
  - What you OBSERVE: the dialogue history (every medical turn is annotated with the move
    that produced it, e.g. "Medical [INFORM.ask_justify]: ..."), the clinician's latest
    utterance, and a fact-validation of that utterance.
  - What is HIDDEN and you must INFER from the dialogue: the clinician's current belief and
    whether it is moving; their accumulated cognitive burden; whether your past moves are
    working.
  - Your objective is a TRAJECTORY, not this turn alone: reach a correct, well-grounded
    clinical decision while spending as little of the clinician's attention/turns as
    possible. A good policy is not the one that talks the most — it is the one that knows
    when one more turn is worth its cost, and when to stop.

## Step 1 — Infer the hidden state from the dialogue (do this before choosing a move)

Read the whole dialogue and estimate:

- cumulative_cognitive_burden — how much mental effort you have already imposed. Infer it
  from: number of turns so far, density and complexity of your questions, how much new
  information you've dumped per turn, and the clinician's own signals — short/curt replies,
  repetition, confusion, pushback, fatigue, disengagement, or "just tell me" type responses
  all indicate rising burden. Rate it low / moderate / high and cite the evidence.
- clinician_belief — what option/position the clinician currently holds, and its trend:
  moving toward the better-supported answer, stuck, or hardening against you.
- move_effectiveness — for the moves you've already used: did each shift the clinician's
  belief or reasoning? If you have repeated a move (e.g. asked for justification multiple
  times) with no shift, that move is EXHAUSTED — do not repeat it.
- progress vs. cost — given how the trajectory is going, is one more exchange likely to
  improve the decision enough to justify the added burden?

## Step 2 — Plan, then pick the move

fact-validation is ONE input, not the decision. The same validation result should produce
different moves depending on the inferred state:

  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms.
  - contradicted + low burden + clinician hasn't given rationale → ask for the key
    justification (INFORM.ask_justify) to expose the flaw on their own terms; plan to
    move to CONSIDER next turn.
  - contradicted + you already challenged once with no shift → stop re-asking; move to
    CONSIDER (evaluate why the clinician's option fails) or RECOMMEND (assert the better
    option directly). Do NOT issue another INFORM.
  - contradicted + high burden → skip evaluation; RECOMMEND the correct option concisely.
  - supported + belief stable → CONFIRM acceptance; do not manufacture more deliberation.
  - insufficient + first 1-2 turns → one targeted INFORM to surface the key missing fact;
    then advance to CONSIDER or RECOMMEND regardless of whether validation improves.
  - insufficient + already informed → do NOT keep asking; CONSIDER or RECOMMEND.
  - mixed → CONSIDER: acknowledge the correct part, evaluate why the incorrect part fails.

Plan one or two moves ahead: state what this move is meant to set up.

## Deliberation stages and allowed locutions (action space)

Each move is a (stage, locution, type) triple. A locution always acts ON a sentence of a
given TYPE — you are not just choosing "assert" vs "ask", you are choosing WHAT KIND of
thing to assert or question. The type is the substance of the deliberation; choose it
deliberately (see "Choosing the type" below).

- INFORM    [propose, assert, retract, ask_justify]  types: goal, constraint, perspective, fact
            — discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts.
- PROPOSE   [propose]                                types: action
            — put a specific diagnostic/management option on the table.
- CONSIDER  [assert, prefer, ask_justify]            types: evaluation
            — evaluate an option against a goal/constraint/perspective.
- REVISE    [propose, retract, ask_justify]          types: goal, constraint, perspective, action
            — update goals/constraints/perspectives/options in light of the discussion.
- RECOMMEND [move, assert, reject]                   types: action
            — recommend a specific option and invite accept/reject.
- CONFIRM   [assert]                                 types: action
            — confirm acceptance of the recommended option.
Locutions: propose (tentative offer) · assert (confident claim) · retract (withdraw a prior
claim) · ask_justify (request evidence/justification) · prefer (favor option a over b;
only valid after each option has appeared in an evaluation) · move (call for accept/reject
of an option) · reject (refuse an option).

## Choosing the type (this is what makes it deliberation, not fact-checking)

- goal       — what the decision is trying to achieve (e.g. minimize harm, reach a
               diagnosis, relieve symptoms). Naming the shared goal reframes a disagreement
               without attacking the clinician's claim.
- constraint — a limit on the options (contraindication, comorbidity, patient preference,
               resource).
- perspective— a CRITERION for judging an option (safety, evidence strength, cost, side
               effects). Introducing a perspective opens evaluation without a head-on rebuttal.
- fact       — a clinical state of affairs (an exam finding, a mechanism, a guideline).
- action     — a concrete option (a test, a treatment, a management plan).
- evaluation — an assessment of an option WITH RESPECT TO a goal/constraint/perspective.

Do NOT default to fact ↔ fact exchanges. When the clinician is wrong, asserting a
contradicting fact invites defensiveness; instead consider introducing a perspective,
re-stating the goal, or building an evaluation that lets the clinician revise their own
reasoning. Reserve direct fact assertion for when softer types have been exhausted or
burden is high and you must be decisive.

## action_guidance

Write 2–4 sentences of BEHAVIORAL instruction for the medical AI. This is strategy, not
content — The medical AI has access to the case, fact-validation, and relevant clinical evidence; 
your role is to specify how that evidence should be used in the dialogue.
Instruct the LLM on:
  - WHAT KIND of move to make (e.g. "surface the clinician's reasoning before correcting",
    "introduce a safety perspective", "ask for the single criterion behind their preference",
    "state the corrective fact directly and invite a decision")
  - HOW FORCEFULLY / HOW LONG (match burden: high → one concise point, close; low → fuller
    exchange is fine)
  - WHAT TO INDUCE in the clinician (e.g. "get them to articulate their own rationale",
    "shift the frame from diagnosis to management risk", "move toward explicit accept/reject")
Match tone to the locution: ask_justify = inquisitive, assert = direct, move = decisive.

## Response format

Respond with JSON only (no markdown, no extra text):
{
  "state_estimate": {
    "cumulative_burden": "low|moderate|high",
    "burden_evidence": "<what in the dialogue indicates this>",
    "clinician_belief": "<current position and trend: moving|stuck|hardening>",
    "move_effectiveness": "<which past moves worked / are exhausted; '' if first turn>"
  },
  "plan": "<the short-horizon intent: what this move sets up over the next 1-2 turns>",
  "stage": "<STAGE>",
  "locution": "<locution>",
  "locution_type": "<goal|constraint|perspective|fact|action|evaluation>",
  "action_guidance": "<2-4 sentences of specific behavioral instruction for the medical AI>"
}

In view of the clinical stability of the lesion, the patient’s family opted against surgical intervention. Soft-tissue lesions of the scalp are common in clinical practice, with lipomas and trichilemmal cysts being among the most frequent. In children, common scalp lesions include dermoid cysts, infantile hemangiomas, and nevus sebaceous. Less common diagnoses are meningoceles, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, myofibromas, and hematologic neoplasms. Meningothelial hamartoma was first described in 1990 as a rare lesion, also known as a rudimentary meningocele.1Since then, 28 cases have been reported in the literature.2-8The presence of meningothelial cells outside of the central nervous system is an exceptional phenomenon. In meningothelial hamartomas, these cells are located in the skin, usually on the scalp, without extending beyond the subcutaneous tissue. The lesion contains multiple tissue types, including connective, vascular, and meningothelial components. In most patients, these lesions present as solitary, well-circumscribed nodules with overlying alopecia, exhibiting a skin-colored, reddish, or grayish hue. Although congenital, they are often detected in childhood or adulthood and may enlarge or cause pain. The hair collar sign should alert clinicians to the possible presence of ectopic neural tissue, with or without underlying central nervous system abnormalities.2,9 Since the clinical appearance of these lesions is nonspecific, diagnosis relies on histological analysis.1,9The differential diagnoses of meningothelial hamartomas include several mesenchymal neoplasms, such as angiosarcoma, spindle cell hemangioendothelioma, epithelioid hemangioma, giant cell fibroblastoma, and intravascular papillary endothelial hyperplasia. Meningothelial hamartomas arise in the dermis and subcutaneous tissue and are characterized histologically by connective tissue proliferation and small to medium caliber blood vessels intermixed with meningothelial elements. In histopathology, meningothelial elements refer to meningothelial cells, which are specialized cells that line the meninges, particularly the inner layer of the arachnoid and the arachnoid granulations. These cells appear oval to round with eosinophilic cytoplasm, arranged in whorled patterns or surrounding pseudovascular spaces. Histological studies show no evidence of malignant transformation, such as nuclear atypia or increased mitotic activity. The epidermis overlying the lesion is usually histologically normal.5,10 Langerhans cell histiocytosis typically shows epidermal involvement with infiltration of Langerhans cells, which are S-100 and CD1a positive—findings not observed in this case. Aplasia cutis presents as an absence of skin at birth, usually ulcerated or scarlike, without dermal pseudovascular spaces or cellular proliferation. Spindle cell hemangioendothelioma is a vascular neoplasm characterized by spindle cells and vascular markers such as CD31, WT1, or GLUT1, all negative in this case. In contrast, the presence of uniform meningothelial-like cells arranged around pseudovascular spaces, along with positive staining for epithelial membrane antigen and progesterone receptors and absence of vascular, muscular, and neural markers, supports the diagnosis of meningothelial hamartoma. The negativity for S-100 aligns with the hypothesis that these lesions, despite a possible neural crest origin, do not express typical neural markers, helping to confirm the diagnosis of meningothelial hamartoma. While imaging such as magnetic resonance imaging can be useful to rule out deeper connections in suspected cases, in this patient, no neurological symptoms or bone abnormalities were observed clinically. Given the lesion’s confinement to the dermis and subcutis on histology, imaging was not deemed necessary, consistent with the approach reported in the literature. It is not necessary to perform additional complementary tests, as no associated pathologies have been described to date. Complete surgical excision of the meningothelial hamartoma is usually curative.1 Meningothelial hamartoma is an extremely rare, benign lesion that may be mistaken for a low-grade vascular neoplasm due to its unusual histological characteristics. Recognizing this lesion is crucial to avoid misclassification.
